_README: The grammar of a journalist-query digest email, kept in data rather than in
code so it can be corrected the day a provider changes its layout without
touching the filtering or drafting logic.
WHAT IS AND IS NOT PROVEN, as of 2026-09-02.
This grammar HAS NOW MET A REAL DIGEST, and the first one it met defeated it.
On 2026-09-02 at 10:33 UTC the first real SOS digest arrived: 17,291
characters, subject '[SOS] Wednesday Morning Media Queries', carrying TEN
queries. The lane parsed TWO of them, raised PARTIAL_DIGEST_PARSE, and went
green -- the stop worked exactly as designed and is the only reason this was
not a silent loss of eight queries.
Three separate defects, all reproduced against the real message, now kept
verbatim-but-redacted at tests/fixtures/journalist-queries/
sos-digest-2026-09-02.eml:
1. SOS separates queries with FIVE underscores. block_delimiters demanded
six or more repeated characters, so the digest never split and the whole
body collapsed into four blocks. parse_block returns at most one query
per block, hence two.
2. Because the blocks did not split, fields CROSSED BETWEEN QUERIES:
query 1's summary was paired with query 6's email address. That is worse
than dropping a query -- it is a draft answering one reporter's question
addressed to a different reporter. Nothing was sent, because this lane
has no send path, but the owner would have been handed it to send.
3. SOS labels the date 'DEADLINE DATE', not 'Deadline', so no deadline was
ever captured, and the unrecognised labels (NAME, MEDIA WEBSITE,
MUCK RACK URL, DEADLINE TIME, TIME ZONE) were appended as continuation
text onto whatever field preceded them.
The fix is `query_start` below: a digest whose queries are introduced by a
numbered SUMMARY line is split on THAT, not on decorative rules, so an
ornamental row of dashes inside one reporter's question can no longer cut a
query in half and a five-underscore separator no longer has to be guessed at.
block_delimiters remains as the fallback for a provider that does not number.
WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT VOLUME, stated by the publisher in the welcome email and
quoted in expected_queries_per_digest below:
- two digests per day, around 6:30am and 1:30pm, occasionally a third;
- typically 10-15 queries per digest, sometimes more;
- Monday to Friday;
- a source replies directly to the reporter.
The 10-15 figure is load-bearing: it is what makes a PARTIAL parse
detectable. A digest that yields two queries when the publisher says it
contains ten or more has dropped eight that nobody knows were there, and
that is worse than refusing outright. It is what caught this.
The dangerous failure is not a parser that breaks; it is a parser that
returns zero, or a handful, from a digest full of queries and gets reported
as 'nothing relevant today'. So an unrecognised message body is a NAMED STOP
called UNPARSEABLE_DIGEST, and a short read is a NAMED STOP called
PARTIAL_DIGEST_PARSE. A quiet day and a broken parser must never look the
same. Neither stop may be removed or loosened to make a run green.

expected_queries_per_digest._source: peter@sourceofsources.com, welcome email, 2026-09-02, verbatim: "They'll contain queries from journalists - typically 10-15 per email, sometimes more if there's a rush."
expected_queries_per_digest._partial_parse_floor_note: A digest that parses to fewer than `partial_parse_floor` queries is reported as PARTIAL_DIGEST_PARSE. Set below the stated low rather than at it: a genuinely light day is possible and should not be a stop, but a digest yielding a couple of queries when ten-plus were sent is a silent drop and must be named.

_why: Not every message from the provider is a query digest. The welcome email is
not, and neither is an unsubscribe confirmation or an account notice. Before
this existed, the welcome email was read as a digest, parsed to zero queries,
and produced UNPARSEABLE_DIGEST -- a false stop that would have fired on
every run for two days and taught its reader to ignore the real one.
Recognition is POSITIVE and declared. A message is only excused from the
digest guard if it MATCHES something here. 'It had no query markers' is not
grounds for excusing it, because that is also exactly what a changed format
looks like -- and excusing that is how the lane would go silently dead.
Each entry needs a subject pattern AND a body marker, so a real digest that
happens to carry a stray phrase is never dismissed.
